title: The Early-Signal List: 12 Buying Signals to Reach Buyers Before Your Competitors
description: 79% of buyers make first contact themselves, about 61% into their journey. 12 early signals, where to find them and the first line to write for each.
lead: This is the full early-signal list from the reel. Most buyers reach out to vendors themselves, and only after doing most of their research. This guide gives you 12 signals that show a company may be starting to buy, where to find each one, and the first line to write so you show up early without spamming.
insider: We build client campaigns around a reason to write, not just a job title. For a construction software client that approach led to **31 sales-qualified demos and 6 signed annual contracts**. Spotting one signal is easy. Checking for them every week and writing to each one fast is what we do for clients.

blocks.text: Why you need to be early

6sense surveyed nearly 4,000 B2B buyers for its [2025 Buyer Experience Report](https://6sense.com/report/buyer-experience/). According to [this summary of the study](https://customerthink.com/research-round-up-6sense-study-provides-critical-insights-on-b2b-buyer-behavior/), **79% of buyers said they made first contact with vendors themselves**, and that first contact came when buyers were about **61% of the way through** their buying process.

The [6sense press release](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20251112018032/en) adds two more numbers. **94% of buying groups ranked their preferred vendors before first contact**, and they bought from that early favorite **77% of the time**. Buyers also had about **16 interactions per person** with the vendor they picked.
Put simply: by the time a buyer calls you, they've mostly decided. If you want a fair chance, you need to be in their head **before** that point.
Worked example: how long buyers research alone
The same press release says buying cycles took about **10 months** in 2025.

items: 10 months × 61% = about **6 months** before the buyer contacts anyone.
That's half a year of reading, comparing and shortlisting without you.

The [study summary](https://customerthink.com/research-round-up-6sense-study-provides-critical-insights-on-b2b-buyer-behavior/) says buying groups filled **4 of 5 shortlist spots on day 1**. Show up late, and you're fighting for one seat.

blocks.text: What a signal is

A signal is a public event that suggests a company may soon need what you sell. A new sales leader, a job post, a new office. It doesn't mean they'll buy. It means you have a **real reason** to write now, and that reason goes in your first line.

blocks.label: Pick 3, not 12
blocks.text: Don't track all 12. Pick the 3 that best match what you sell. A bookkeeping firm should watch funding and new locations. A recruiting firm should watch job posts.
How to use it, step by step

items: **Pick 3 signals** that clearly connect to your offer. Ask: if this happened, would they need me more?
**Set a weekly check.** Same day each week, look for new signals in your target list. Write them in a sheet: company, signal, date, link.
**Write within days, not months.** A signal from last week is a reason. A signal from last year is old news. A common rule is to write within 1 to 2 weeks.
**Put the reason in your first line.** "Saw you just opened a Denver office" earns the next line. A generic opener doesn't.
**Connect the signal to the problem.** Don't just say congrats. Say what that event usually brings: "New offices usually mean..."
**One signal = one campaign.** Write a different email for each signal type, so the reason always fits.

blocks.text: First lines for each type of signal
New leader
Congrats on the new role at [company]. Most new [role]s I talk to spend their first 90 days fixing [problem].
Job post
Saw you're hiring a [role]. While that seat is open, who's covering [the task]?
New location
Saw [company] just opened in [city]. New locations usually need [result] before the local word of mouth kicks in.

blocks.text: Write the email with Claude

blocks.label: Signal email prompt
blocks.text:
I sell: [your offer, one sentence]
My best result: [a real result, or "none yet"]

Here is a company and the signal I found:
Company: [name]
Person: [name, role]
Signal: [what happened, with the date and link]

Write a cold email under 70 words:
- First line: the signal, said simply and kindly. No "I hope this finds you well".
- Second line: the problem this signal usually brings for a company like theirs.
- Third line: one line of proof (use my result only if it's real; if "none yet", offer something useful for free).
- End with one easy question, like "Worth a look?"
Plain, simple English. Don't invent facts about the company.

blocks.label: Weekly signal sheet columns
blocks.text: Company | Person | Signal type | What happened | Date found | Link | Email sent (date) | Reply?

blocks.label: The rule
blocks.text: It won't work unless the reason is in your first line.

faq.q: Does a signal mean they're ready to buy?
faq.a: No. It means you have a good reason to write now. Many will say not yet. That's fine: ask when to check back.

faq.q: Do I need paid tools to find signals?
faq.a: No. Careers pages, LinkedIn, Google News and press releases are free. Paid tools just save time when your list gets big.

faq.q: How many signals should I track?
faq.a: Start with 3 that clearly connect to your offer. Add more only when those are running every week.

faq.q: Isn't it creepy to mention their news?
faq.a: Not if it's public and you say it kindly. Hiring posts and new offices are things companies want people to see.
